extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating long-form fiction (novels/short novels) focused on how to use setting, pictorial description, point of view, and pacing to make drama credible and to convey time, character, and energy. Emphasises techniques used by Balzac, Dickens, Stevenson and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placing a figure in its surroundings
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac's power of placing a figure in its surroundings — he cannot think of his people without the homes they inhabit; to imagine a human being is to imagine a province, a city, a corner of the city, a building at a turn of the street, certain furnished rooms, and finally the man or woman who lives in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe approach to doorway, passage to staircase, placement of parlour-chairs, vases on mantelpiece, pots and pans etc. These descriptions are 'offered as an essential preliminary to the story, a matter that must obviously be dealt with, once for all, before the story can proceed.' Examples: Maison Vauquer, Maison Grandet, Eugenie Grandet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting as provision of character and energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparatory picture is not merely a stage-setting but 'a provision of character and energy for the drama when it begins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the background to supply temperament, motives and momentum for action so that when the drama starts it carries the weight of its setting (e.g., Goriot carrying the daily experience of the Maison Vauquer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisurely massing of pictorial impression before action
rubrics_metrics.description: Massing the force which is presently to drive the drama on its way — building a reserve of vigour in the picture before precipitating action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time to build up a fully created impression of place and people so the subsequent action benefits from an already-established world, rather than rushing immediately into plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economical preparation of scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac's care in creating the scene is 'truly economical' — preparatory pictures are as important as the events they enclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in thorough early scene-building so later narrative can be concise; the apparent verbosity is purposeful and ultimately economical with dramatic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed factual description vs. indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: An author may appear to 'abandon himself to a craving for facts' and be guilty of a 'lust of description for its own sake'; this is sometimes tiresome but can still result in an effective scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid needless piling up of detail unless you genuinely possess the image; when executed with real knowledge the lengthy research produces a scene in which action can move 'as rapidly as he chooses' without losing emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial impression wrought to the right pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial impression, 'wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama— will become an effective agency in the book, instead of remaining the mere decorative introduction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate descriptive intensity: enough to authenticate and energize the drama, but not so much that picture overwhelms or becomes mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression of crowds, events and time into short books
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac could 'pack into a short book ... such an effect of crowds and events, above all such an effect of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concentrated pictorial and factual groundwork to imply breadth of experience and passage of time without sprawling length; compression arises from a well-prepared scene more than from interweaving continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distracting cross-book associations
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters recur from one book to another, irrelevant backstory (e.g., Delphine's past in Lucien's story) can 'detract' and 'disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using recurring characters, ensure they 'shed their irrelevant life' for the present story; include only the elements of their past that directly serve the foreground action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of background to absorb and legitimize romance or marvels
rubrics_metrics.description: If an extravagant or romantic tale can be 'firmly embedded in a background of truth, its falsity may be disguised' and the whole accepted as reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed unlikely events in a credible, truthful setting to make them plausible; beware of a 'gaudy' romance clashing with too-sober realism (Balzac's difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain overcharged or incredible drama by pictorial art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where action 'is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic... it is made to look less so... by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soften or qualify extremes of plot by surrounding them with credible, detailed scene and life, so the drama appears more believable and less sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce violent or romantic intrigue gradually through populated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens' method: lead gradually into romantic intrigues 'through well-populated scenes of character and humour; so that his world is actual... by the time that his plot begins to thicken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a broad, lively panorama before concentrating on the central extraordinary action — it vouches for the action and compels belief (examples: Bleak House, Dombey and Son).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer scenic action and dialogue over general narrative for vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens is 'always readier to work in action and dialogue than to describe at large; he is happier in placing a character there before us, as the man or woman talked and behaved in a certain hour, on a certain spot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show character through immediate scenes and speech rather than long summary when aiming for dramatic vividness; reserve summary only when intentional and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize characters sharply in limited scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters appear only incidentally in scenes, the novelist 'is forced to crystallize and formulate his characters very sharply' and may resort to 'labelling his people with a trick or a phrase.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dramatised presentation with few appearances, distill characters to distinctive traits or memorable phrasing so they register quickly and reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of narrative method modulates pictorial vs dramatic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of first person or other narrators changes the balance: e.g., first-person may 'enhance' a plain narrative into drama or, in another subject, 'thrust the book ... towards the pictured impression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select point-of-view deliberately to tune whether the work leans toward intimate dramatization or toward a framed pictorial impression; different subjects call for different effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and fullness of detail as an essential preliminary
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac 'imposes his belief in the need for precision and fullness; Balzac is so sure that every detail must be known... that his reader cannot begin to question it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can truly imagine the scene in detail, present it plainly and fully (even inventory-like); this secures the context so later concision still feels authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scene to imply passage of time and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough preliminary picture can 'include the representation of time' so that later statements like 'Five years went by in this way' are credible because 'we already see them opening and closing upon the girl.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare durable, repeating elements (routine, surroundings, social texture) that allow you to skip long spans of time without losing the sense of duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle low-incident stories via interior focalization or pictorial groundwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 'there is so little in the way of incident' a novelist might either follow the character's consciousness in detail to show time, or, as Balzac does, prepare an external picture so the passage of years is implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to fill sparse material by intense interior narration (show the slow flow of feeling) or by creating a persistent external world that makes the years comprehensible at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical listing of facts unless author truly possesses the image
rubrics_metrics.description: A different kind of writer attempting Balzac's method 'would have to feel his way tentatively... his account would consist of that mechanical sum of details which makes no image.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't substitute quantity of detail for authentic, coherent vision; only a writer who 'knows everything' about a place can itemize facts and still produce a telling overall impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend an opening episode when it embodies the character's chief experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac 'extends his account of [the opening episode] so far ... that he has written two thirds of the book by the time the young man is finally despatched to the Indies' — making the brief romance itself the main lived event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a short incident encapsulates a character's whole life or emotional centre, it can legitimately be made large in proportion to its factual duration so it carries the weight of the narrative.
